entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16768"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1-1Cor.2.16">1Co 2:1-16</reference>. Paul's Subject of Preaching, Christ Crucified, Not in Worldly, but in Heavenly, Wisdom among the Perfect.<div eID="gen33004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16768"/><hi type="bold">1. And I--</hi>"So I" [Conybeare] as one of the "foolish, weak, and despised" instruments employed by God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">28</reference>); "glorying in the Lord," not in man's wisdom (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">1Co 1:31</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23">1Co 1:23</reference>, "We."<div eID="gen33005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when I came--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.18.1">Ac 18:1</reference>, &c.). Paul might, had he pleased, have used an ornate style, having studied secular learning at Tarsus of Cilicia, which Strabo preferred as a school of learning to Athens or Alexandria; here, doubtless, he read the Cilician Aratus' poems (which he quotes, <reference osisRef="Acts.17.28">Ac 17:28</reference>), and Epimenides (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>), and Menander (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.33">1Co 15:33</reference>). Grecian intellectual development was an important element in preparing the way for the Gospel, but it failed to regenerate the world, showing that for this a superhuman power is needed. Hellenistic (Grecizing) Judaism at Tarsus and Alexandria was the connecting link between the schools of Athens and those of the Rabbis. No more fitting birthplace could there have been for the apostle of the Gentiles than Tarsus, free as it was from the warping influences of Rome, Alexandria, and Athens. He had at the same time Roman citizenship, which protected him from sudden violence. Again, he was reared in the Hebrew divine law at Jerusalem. Thus, as the three elements, Greek cultivation, Roman polity (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Lu 2:1</reference>), and the divine law given to the Jews, combined just at Christ's time, to prepare the world for the Gospel, so the same three, by God's marvellous providence, met together in the apostle to the Gentiles [Conybeare and Howson].<div eID="gen33006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">testimony of God--</hi>"the testimony of Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">1Co 1:6</reference>); therefore Christ is God. <div eID="gen33007" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16769"/><div sID="gen33008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16769"/>2. The Greek implies, "The only definite thing that I made it my business to know among you, was to know Jesus Christ (His person) and Him crucified (His office)" [Alford], not exalted on the earthly throne of David, but executed as the vilest malefactor. The historical fact of Christ's crucifixion had probably been put less prominently forward by the seekers after human wisdom in the Corinthian church, to avoid offending learned heathens and Jews. Christ's person and Christ's office constitute the sum of the Gospel. <div eID="gen33008" type="x-p"/>

I--</hi>the preacher: as <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1Co 2:2</reference> describes the subject, "Christ crucified," and <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">1Co 2:4</reference> the mode of preaching: "my speech ... not with enticing words," "but in demonstration of the Spirit."<div eID="gen33009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weakness--</hi>personal and bodily (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen33010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trembling--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Phil.2.12">Php 2:12</reference>). Not personal fear, but a trembling anxiety to perform a duty; anxious conscientiousness, as proved by the contrast to "eye service" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>) [Conybeare and Howson]. <div eID="gen33011" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16773"/><div sID="gen33018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16773"/>6-7. Yet the Gospel preaching, so far from being at variance with true "wisdom," is a wisdom infinitely higher than that of the wise of the world.<div eID="gen33018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we speak--</hi>resuming "we" (preachers, I, Apollos, &c.) from "we preach" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>), only that here, "we speak" refers to something less public (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>, "mystery ... hidden") than "we preach," which is public. For "wisdom" here denotes not the whole of Christian doctrine, but its sublimer and deeper principles.<div eID="gen33019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perfect--</hi>Those matured in Christian experience and knowledge alone can understand the true superiority of the Christian wisdom which Paul preached. Distinguished not only from worldly and natural men, but also from babes, who though "in Christ" retain much that is "carnal" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Co 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.2">2</reference>), and cannot therefore understand the deeper truths of Christianity (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">1Co 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">Php 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">He 5:14</reference>). Paul does not mean by the "mystery" or "hidden wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>) some hidden tradition distinct from the Gospel (like the Church of Rome's disciplina arcani and doctrine of reserve), but the unfolding of the treasures of knowledge, once hidden in God's counsels, but now announced to all, which would be intelligently comprehended in proportion as the hearer's inner life became perfectly transformed into the image of Christ. Compare instances of such "mysteries," that is, deeper Christian truths, not preached at Paul's first coming to Corinth, when he confined himself to the fundamental elements (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1Co 2:2</reference>), but now spoken to the "perfect" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.51">1Co 15:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.25">Ro 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.5">Ep 3:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">6</reference>). "Perfect" is used not of absolute perfection, but relatively to "babes," or those less ripe in Christian growth (compare <reference osisRef="Phil.3.12">Php 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.15">15</reference>, with <reference osisRef="1John.2.12-1John.2.14">1Jo 2:12-14</reference>). "God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7">1Co 2:7</reference>) is opposed to the world, the apostles to "the princes [great and learned men] of this world" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">1Co 1:20</reference>) [Bengel].<div eID="gen33020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to naught--</hi>nothingness (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>). They are transient, not immortal. Therefore, their wisdom is not real [Bengel]. Rather, translate with Alford, "Which are being brought to naught," namely, by God's choosing the "things which are not (the weak and despised things of the Gospel), to bring to naught (the same verb as here) things that are" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.28">1Co 1:28</reference>). <div eID="gen33021" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16776"/><div sID="gen33029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16776"/><hi type="bold">9. But--</hi>(it has happened) as it is written.<div eID="gen33029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33030" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eye hath not seen, &c.--</hi>Alford translates, "The things which eye saw not ... the things which God prepared ... to us God revealed through His Spirit." Thus, however, the "but" of <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference> is ignored. Rather construe, as Estius, "('We speak,' supplied from <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>), things which eye saw not (heretofore), ... things which God prepared ... But God revealed them to us," &c. The quotation is not a verbatim one, but an inspired exposition of the "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, from <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Is 64:4</reference>). The exceptive words, "O God, beside (that is, except) Thee," are not quoted directly, but are virtually expressed in the exposition of them (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:10</reference>), "None but thou, O God, seest these mysteries, and God hath revealed them to us by His Spirit."<div eID="gen33030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entered--</hi>literally, "come up into the heart." A Hebraism (compare, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jr 3:16</reference>, Margin). In <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Is 64:4</reference> it is "Prepared (literally, 'will do') for him that waiteth for Him"; here, "for them that love Him." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16780"/><div sID="gen33041" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16780"/><hi type="bold">13. also--</hi>We not only know by the Holy Ghost, but we also speak the "things freely given to us of God" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.12">1Co 2:12</reference>).<div eID="gen33041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which the Holy Ghost teacheth--</hi>The old manuscripts read "the Spirit" simply, without "Holy."<div eID="gen33042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comparing spiritual things with spiritual--</hi>expounding the Spirit-inspired Old Testament Scripture, by comparison with the Gospel which Jesus by the same Spirit revealed [Grotius]; and conversely illustrating the Gospel mysteries by comparing them with the Old Testament types [Chrysostom]. So the Greek word is translated, "comparing" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.12">2Co 10:12</reference>). Wahl (Key of the New Testament) translates, "explaining (as the Greek is translated, <reference osisRef="Gen.40.8">Ge 40:8</reference>, the Septuagint) to spiritual (that is, Spirit-taught) men, spiritual things (the things which we ourselves are taught by the Spirit)." Spirit-taught men alone can comprehend spiritual truths. This accords with <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1Co 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.10">9, 10</reference>, 14, 15; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">1Co 3:1</reference>. Alford translates, "Putting together (combining) spirituals with spirituals"; that is, attaching spiritual words to spiritual things, which we should not do, if we were to use words of worldly wisdom to expound spiritual things (so <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1">1Co 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1Pe 4:11</reference>). Perhaps the generality of the neuters is designed to comprehend these several notions by implication. Comparing, or combining, spirituals with spirituals; implying both that spiritual things are only suited to spiritual persons (so "things" comprehended persons, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1Co 1:27</reference>), and also that spiritual truths can only be combined with spiritual (not worldly-wise) words; and lastly, spirituals of the Old and New Testaments can only be understood by mutual comparison or combination, not by combination with worldly "wisdom," or natural perceptions (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1Co 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.4-2Cor.1.9">2:1, 4-9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.119.18">Psa 119:18</reference>). <div eID="gen33043" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16781"/><div sID="gen33044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16781"/><hi type="bold">14. natural man--</hi>literally, "a man of animal soul." As contrasted with the spiritual man, he is governed by the animal soul, which overbears his spirit, which latter is without the Spirit of God (Jude 19). The carnal man (the man led by bodily appetites, and also by a self-exalting spirit, estranged from the divine life) is closely akin; so too the "earthly." "Devilish," or "demon-like"; "led by an evil spirit," is the awful character of such a one, in its worst type (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receiveth not--</hi>though they are offered to him, and are "worthy of being received by all men" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen33045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33046" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are foolishness unto him--</hi>whereas he seeks "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">1Co 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen33046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither can he--</hi>Not only does he not, but he cannot know them, and therefore has no wish to "receive" them (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.7">Ro 8:7</reference>). <div eID="gen33047" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16782"/><div sID="gen33048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16782"/><hi type="bold">15. He that is spiritual--</hi>literally, "the spiritual (man)." In <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>, it is "A [not 'the,' as English Version] natural man." The spiritual is the man distinguished above his fellow men, as he in whom the Spirit rules. In the unregenerate, the spirit which ought to be the organ of the Holy Spirit (and which is so in the regenerate), is overridden by the animal soul, and is in abeyance, so that such a one is never called "spiritual."<div eID="gen33048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgeth all things--</hi>and persons, by their true standard (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2-1Cor.6.4">1Co 6:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1Jo 4:1</reference>), in so far as he is spiritual. "Discerneth ... is discerned," would better accord with the translation of the same Greek (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>). Otherwise for "discerned," in <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.14">1Co 2:14</reference>, translate, "judged of," to accord with the translation, "judgeth ... is judged" in this fifteenth verse. He has a practical insight into the verities of the Gospel, though he is not infallible on all theoretical points. If an individual may have the Spirit without being infallible, why may not the Church have the Spirit, and yet not be infallible (a refutation of the plea of Rome for the Church's infallibility, from <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>)? As the believer and the Church have the Spirit, and are yet not therefore impeccable, so he and the Church have the Spirit, and yet are not infallible or impeccable. He and the Church are both infallible and impeccable, only in proportion to the degree in which they are led by the Spirit. The Spirit leads into all truth and holiness; but His influence on believers and on the Church is as yet partial. Jesus alone, who had the Spirit without measure (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>), is both infallible and impeccable. Scripture, because it was written by men, who while writing were infallibly inspired, is unmixed truth (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.5">Pr 28:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.27">1Jo 2:27</reference>). <div eID="gen33049" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 15. He that is spiritual-- literally, "the spiritual (man)." In 1Co 2:14 , it is "A [not 'the,' as English Version] natural man." The spiritual is the man distinguished above his fellow men, as he in whom the Spirit rules. In the unregenerate, the spirit which ought to be the organ of the Holy Spirit (and which is so in the regenerate), is overridden by the animal soul, and is in abeyance, so that such a one is never called "spiritual." judgeth all things-- and persons, by their true standard (compare 1Co 6:2-4 ; 1Jo 4:1 ), in so far as he is spiritual. "Discerneth ... is discerned," would better accord with the translation of the same Greek ( 1Co 2:14 ). Otherwise for "discerned," in 1Co 2:14 , translate, "judged of," to accord with the translation, "judgeth ... is judged" in this fifteenth verse. He has a practical insight into the verities of the Gospel, though he is not infallible on all theoretical points. If an individual may have the Spirit without being infallible, why may not the Church have the Spirit, and yet not be infallible (a refutation of the plea of Rome for the Church's infallibility, from Mt 28:20 ; Joh 16:13 )? As the believer and the Church have the Spirit, and are yet not therefore impeccable, so he and the Church have the Spirit, and yet are not infallible or impeccable. He and the Church are both infallible and impeccable, only in proportion to the degree in which they are led by the Spirit. The Spirit leads into all truth and holiness; but His influence on believers and on the Church is as yet partial. Jesus alone, who had the Spirit without measure ( Joh 3:34 ), is both infallible and impeccable. Scripture, because it was written by men, who while writing were infallibly inspired, is unmixed truth ( Pr 28:5 ; 1Jo 2:27 ).

entries.content_plain: 16. For-- proof of 1Co 2:15 , that the spiritual man "is judged of no man." In order to judge the spiritual man, the ordinary man must "know the mind of the Lord." But "who of ordinary men knows" that? that he may instruct him-- that is, so as to be able to set Him right as His counsellor (quoted from Is 40:13 , 14 ). So the Septuagint translates the Greek verb, which means to "prove," in Ac 9:22 . Natural men who judge spiritual men, living according to the mind of God ("We have the mind of Christ"), are virtually wishing to instruct God, and bring Him to another mind, as counsellors setting to right their king. we have the mind of Christ-- in our degree of capability to apprehend it. Is 40:13 , 14 refers to Jehovah: therefore, as it is applied here to Christ, He is Jehovah.
